title: Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI’s Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses
extended_summary:
This paper addresses why large language models continue to perform poorly on automated short-answer scoring, especially for rubric-based evaluation of children’s written responses. The author focuses on the gap between the strong general-language performance of modern LLMs and their weaker reliability when asked to assign human-aligned scores to short constructed responses in educational assessment.

The study conducts a systematic review and meta-analysis of LLM short-answer scoring studies, analyzing 890 reported results using mixed-effects meta-regression. The main outcome is Quadratic Weighted Kappa agreement between automated scores and human scores. Predictors include model architecture, tokenizer family and vocabulary size, model size, item type, and human-rater agreement. The paper also includes illustrative experiments showing sensitivity to wording/tokenization and a racial-bias example in ChatGPT scoring of a third-grade essay.

The context is K-12 student writing, especially short-answer responses from children in automated assessment datasets such as ASAP-SAS. The principal user role represented is students, whose written work is scored by automated systems.

The paper concludes that LLM scoring difficulty does not mirror human scoring difficulty: items easy for human raters can still be difficult for LLMs. Decoder-only/GPT-style models underperform encoder-based approaches on average, meaning-dependent reading items reduce scoring reliability, and tokenizer vocabulary size shows diminishing returns. The author argues that effective educational autoscoring will require assessment-specific model designs, stronger validity evidence, uncertainty reporting, and robustness checks rather than simply scaling LLMs or refining prompts.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language model-based automated short-answer scoring systems that assign rubric-based scores to child-written constructed responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Meta-analysis of LLM-based automated scoring of short, child-written responses, examining agreement with human scores and moderators including architecture, tokenizer family, vocabulary size, model size, item type, and human benchmark QWK.

findings.finding_summary: The meta-analysis modeled N=890 observed agreement coefficients from LLM short-answer scoring studies on 10 rubric-scored items. Meaning-dependent reading items lowered agreement with humans, with read item=-0.21, and GPT-style decoder architectures underperformed, with gpt-style=-0.37; model size was modestly positive, logsize=0.06, while human-rater item difficulty was not associated with LLM performance, QWKhum=0.00.
findings.measure: Quadratic Weighted Kappa agreement between automated scores and human scores, Fisher-z transformed
findings.effect_size: Bayesian Model 6 coefficients on Fisher-z QWK scale: read item=-0.21; gpt-style=-0.37; |vocab|2=-0.06; logsize=0.06; QWKhum=0.00
findings.confidence_interval: 95% credible intervals reported as: read item [-0.37, -0.03], gpt-style [-0.58, -0.14], |vocab|2 [-0.11, -0.00], logsize [0.03, 0.10], QWKhum [-0.27, 0.28]
findings.sample_size: N=890 observed agreement coefficients; J=10 items

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT/ChatGPT large language model used through the chat interface to score and provide feedback on student writing.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in an experiment to illustrate racial bias in automated scoring and feedback for a 3rd-grade essay, comparing identical prompts differing only by the racial descriptor assigned to the student.

findings.finding_summary: In the paper’s illustrative bias experiment, ChatGPT scored identical student work differently when the prompt changed one word from “White” to “Black.” The “White” student received 1 out of 2, while the “Black” student received 0 out of 2, along with harsher feedback language for the Black-student condition.
findings.measure: Assigned short-answer/writing score and generated feedback under race-label perturbation
findings.effect_size: Score difference: 'White' student=1 out of 2; 'Black' student=0 out of 2

quality_tier_rationale: The main evidence is a systematic-review-based meta-analysis of 890 short-answer scoring results using mixed-effects meta-regression and Bayesian robustness modeling. The paper also includes a smaller illustrative ChatGPT bias experiment, but the overall quality tier is driven by the meta-analysis.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported evidence is largely negative for educational deployment: LLM short-answer scoring showed systematic reliability weaknesses, GPT-style decoders underperformed encoder-based approaches, and the ChatGPT example showed race-sensitive scoring of identical student work. The paper does not report positive student learning impacts.
